posts.title: A recovery route should remove the next friction

copy.default:
A recovery message is only useful if the next step is easier than the problem it is trying to solve.

If an enquiry stalled, can the person resume without repeating everything?

If an appointment was cancelled, is rebooking clear?

If a client is due to return, can they choose an appropriate route without searching for it?

If a staff member needs to help, does the system make that handoff obvious?

The message can be well written and still fail operationally when the route behind it creates more work.

Good follow-up reduces uncertainty.

A good recovery route also reduces the friction between deciding and doing.

posts.title: A live journey needs an exception check

copy.default:
A lifecycle journey can stay switched on while the business around it changes.

A service is renamed.
A booking route moves.
A team member takes on a different responsibility.
A new offer changes who should enter.
A customer reply no longer reaches the right person.

None of those changes has to break the automation completely.

The journey may continue sending while becoming less relevant or harder to act on.

That is why a useful operating review should look for exceptions, not only failures.

What changed since the journey was approved?

What assumption is no longer true?

What needs to be updated before the system becomes a quiet source of friction?

posts.title: Lesson: choose the comparison before judging the journey

copy.default:
Retention School: Choose the comparison before judging the journey

A result is hard to interpret when the comparison is selected afterwards.

Before a lifecycle test begins, define:

What customer state is being measured.
What outcome matches the job.
How long the response window should be.
What historical or control comparison is fair.
What changes in season, offer or channel could distort the result.

Then keep those rules stable long enough to learn something useful.

The aim is not to force certainty from a small test.

It is to make sure the next decision is based on a comparison that was designed before the outcome was known.
